news.2026-10-13-cuba-solaire-blocus.titl: Cut off from oil by Washington, Cuba covers itself in Chinese solar panels
news.2026-10-13-cuba-solaire-blocus.summ: With the US oil blockade, Cuba no longer has enough fuel for its power plants. The island is betting on the sun, with China's help, but solar still does not cover its needs.
news.2026-10-13-cuba-solaire-blocus.poin: According to data from the research centre Ember, Chinese exports of solar panels to Cuba rose from about $3 million in 2023 to $117 million in 2025 [1].

A deal with China provides for 92 solar parks across the country by 2028; about 50 were already running by mid-2026, and Cuba has pledged to reach at least 24% renewable energy by 2030 [1]. Solar would supply about 10% of electricity, up from nearly 3% in 2024 [1].

This rush to solar follows an order signed on 29 January 2026 by Donald Trump, which opens the way to tariffs on countries that supply oil to Cuba [3]. Cuba has also cut transport and reduced opening hours of schools and workplaces [2].
When a country can no longer buy its fuel, it has to produce its own energy. Cuba is doing it with what it has: cheap Chinese panels, installed at full speed.

But the parks are small and scattered across the island, the sun does not shine every day and storage is lacking: experts say solar cannot yet cover peak consumption, and the country still depends heavily on fossil fuels [1].
It is also an example of how a US sanction can push a country toward China: Beijing supplies the panels, Washington cuts the oil.
news.2026-10-13-cuba-solaire-blocus.forM: Cuba is an extreme case, but it shows what happens when energy becomes a weapon: everyone looks for a source they control. The same reasoning pushes Europe to bet on solar and wind, and it explains why China sells so many panels around the world.

Africa launches its own rating agency to judge its debts differently
Inaugurated in Mauritius on 7 October, the Africa Credit Rating Agency wants to challenge the ratings of the Western giants, which African states say cost them too much in interest.
The Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) was inaugurated on Wednesday 7 October 2026 in Balaclava, north of Port Louis, in Mauritius, where it is headquartered [1].
It is to give credit opinions on states, companies, local authorities and institutions, focusing mainly on local-currency debt; it will not be owned by African governments [1].

African governments accuse existing agencies of imposing a “prejudice premium” that raises their borrowing costs; Ghana and Zambia say rating downgrades made their debt crises worse [1]. The chair of the African Union Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, warned against expecting an immediate drop in the cost of money [1].
An agency's rating decides the rate at which a country can borrow: the lower the rating, the higher the interest. For countries already in debt, a few percentage points weigh heavily.
The idea behind AfCRA is to offer another view, closer to the ground. The challenge will be to convince investors: an agency is only worth something if lenders believe its ratings.
The launch follows a public dispute between the African Peer Review Mechanism and the agency Fitch, after the downgrade of the bank Afreximbank; Fitch defends its method [1].
Agency ratings influence debt rates for every country, France included. Seeing Africa create its own shows that this power, long held by a few Western companies, is increasingly challenged.
inauguration of the agency in Mauritius, a year later than originally planned
news.2026-10-13-nigeria-opay-bourse-new-: Nigeria: OPay, the fintech that went from loss to profit, eyes the New York stock exchange
The mobile payments company OPay filed for a New York listing on 9 October. It shows rising profits, but also risks in its investments.

On 9 October OPay filed an IPO document (Form F-1) with the US regulator (SEC) to list its shares in New York under the ticker OPAY, targeting a valuation of about $4 billion; no listing date is confirmed [1][2].

According to the filing, net profit reached $90.9 million in the first half of 2026, up from $21.7 million a year earlier, on $467.1 million in revenue [2]. In 2025 the company earned $72.47 million, after a $50.98 million loss in 2024 [3].
The filing also flags a short-term investment portfolio of $532.9 million at 30 June 2026, which carries liquidity and counterparty risks [1].
OPay is one of the apps replacing the bank for millions of Nigerians: payments, transfers, small loans. Its arrival in New York would be a strong signal for African finance.

But these figures come from the company's own filing and the press, and net profit differs from the loss attributed to ordinary shareholders because of non-cash items [3]. Investors will therefore look closely.

When a payment app born in Lagos can raise billions in New York, it shows that African mobile finance now carries weight in the global economy. It is the same movement as the phone payments that grew in China or India.

news.2026-10-13-turquie-bulgarie-chemin-: A new railway to the Bulgarian border: Europe paid €275 million to open the road to Central Asia
Türkiye inaugurated on 9 October a railway section towards Bulgaria, partly funded by the European Union. It is meant to ease the “Middle Corridor” between Europe and Central Asia.

On 9 October, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and European Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos inaugurated the Çerkezköy–Kapıkule section, about 153 km long, part of the Halkalı–Kapıkule line to the Bulgarian border [1][2].

The European Union provided a €275 million grant through its pre-accession assistance instrument (IPA II); the Commission calls it the largest infrastructure project to date in EU-Türkiye cooperation [1]. The grant had been announced in 2019 [3].

The Commission expects shorter transit times on the “Middle Corridor”, the freight route between Europe and Central Asia via the Caucasus; the Astana Times mentions better freight capacity at the western end of this corridor [2].
The Middle Corridor is the freight route linking Central Asia to Europe across the Caspian Sea, the Caucasus and then Türkiye. Every link that is too slow holds back everything else.
The Commission presents this line as the first concrete result of its programme of connections with Central Asia through the South Caucasus [2].
Figures vary by source: the announced length ranges from 153 to 189 km depending on the section counted, and the total cost is not always the same [1][3].

When a faster route opens between Asia and Europe, the price and delivery time of some products can change. Türkiye, already a key country for trade between the two continents, gains even more weight with Brussels.

news.2026-10-13-kazakhstan-cable-caspien: An internet cable on the bed of the Caspian Sea links Kazakhstan to Azerbaijan
The cable is laid between Aktau and Sumqayit. It is to offer a capacity of over 400 terabits per second, but its start date remains unclear.
Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have finished laying the fibre-optic cable on the bed of the Caspian Sea; it reached the Kazakh coast in early August 2026, and work continues onshore [1].
It is designed for over 400 terabits per second and run by the joint venture CaspiLink B.V.; its length is given as 380 km on the Azerbaijani side and 390 km on the Kazakh side [1].

According to Kazakhstan's Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, it is due to enter service in October 2026 [2], while JAM News speaks of commercial operation by the end of the year [3].
The internet runs on cables. Linking the two shores of the Caspian opens a new direct route between Central Asia and the Caucasus.
Analysts see a change in Eurasia's digital geography [3].
Caution is needed: at the time of the latest information, the start of service was not confirmed.
The services you use (video, cloud, games) travel through cables of this kind. The more there are, the more resilient the network is in case of a breakdown.

news.2026-10-13-arabie-forum-energie-riy: Riyadh gathers the world's energy ministers despite bombs at its airport
The International Energy Forum was held in Riyadh on 11 October, just after the city's airport was targeted. Egypt and Saudi Arabia signed an oil and gas agreement.

The 17th ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum (IEF17) was held on Sunday 11 October in Riyadh, under the theme “Energy Security and Shared Goals in a New Era”; it opened an energy week that also includes the World Petroleum Congress [1][2].

According to an Iraqi report, the conference went ahead despite bombings at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, which Saudi officials blame on Yemen's Houthis, and it welcomed the announced return of the United States to the Forum [2].

After the meeting, Egypt's Petroleum Minister Karim Badawi and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed a memorandum of understanding on the trade, transport, storage and distribution of crude oil, petroleum products and gas [3].
When the Strait of Hormuz is under threat, the question is no longer just the price of oil but its security: where it passes, who can protect it, who can store it.

That the meeting took place despite the attacks shows that Saudi Arabia wants to present itself as a stable hub of global energy. The announced return of the United States to the body strengthens it, but it rests on a single report, to be confirmed.

Decisions taken at these meetings weigh on the price of fuel and gas in France. Agreements between producing and consuming countries are the discreet side of what is also at stake in the Strait of Hormuz.

news.2026-10-13-cambodge-croissance-tour: Cambodia: tourists stay away and growth falls to 3.5%
The World Bank lowered its forecast for Cambodia on 6 October. Fewer foreign visitors and more expensive fuel are weighing on households.

On 6 October, the World Bank lowered its 2026 growth forecast for Cambodia to 3.5%, from 5.3% last year; it had set it at 3.9% in April and 4.3% in January [1][3]. It cites the drop in foreign tourist arrivals, lower remittances from migrants and higher oil prices [1].
Tourist arrivals reportedly fell 44% to 2.25 million over the first eight months of 2026, which the press links to online scams, tensions on the border with Thailand and conflicts in West Asia [2].
At the end of September, the IMF forecast 3% growth and 5.6% inflation for 2026; the World Bank expects a rebound to 4% in 2027 and then 5% in 2028 [1][2].
Cambodia lives largely off tourism and clothing. When visitors come less, hotels, restaurants and small shops suffer.
Exports of clothing, footwear and travel goods are holding up: they rose 7.2% over a year, to $11.76 billion over eight months [2]. The economy is not collapsing, but it rests on few engines.
The recovery scenario assumes that energy prices calm down and tourism returns [1].

If you wear a garment made in Cambodia, it is one of the products that keeps the country's economy going. And the idea that an energy crisis on the other side of the world can cut tourism in Southeast Asia affects you if you travel.

news.2026-10-13-panama-seisme-canal.titl: 7.7 earthquake in Panama: the canal holds, but losses could reach 10% of GDP
news.2026-10-13-panama-seisme-canal.summ: An earthquake struck the south of the country on Friday 9 October. The great trade route of the world was not interrupted, but the country suffered outages and closures.
news.2026-10-13-panama-seisme-canal.poin: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday 9 October, at a depth of about 12.6 km, according to the USGS (the US Geological Survey); tsunami alerts were issued for the Pacific coast of several Central and South American countries [1][3].

The Canal Authority said the canal was operating normally and that ships were passing without interruption; about 90 vessels were waiting at both ends, according to LSEG data, which suggests slowed rather than stopped traffic [1].
Power was cut in six provinces and Tocumen International Airport suspended flights before reopening [2]. The USGS estimates that economic losses could amount to 1% to 10% of Panama's GDP [1].
The Panama Canal carries part of world trade. An earthquake this violent could have stopped it; it did not, which reassures shipowners.

What remains is the shock to the country itself: damaged buildings, power cuts, suspended flights. The USGS range is very wide, from 1% to 10% of GDP, which shows the uncertainty about the real extent of the damage.
Early information remains partial: no official damage assessment had been published.
news.2026-10-13-panama-seisme-canal.forM: Many products you buy (cars, electronics, energy) pass through the canal. Had it closed, delays and prices could have risen; its smooth running avoids, for now, a new global traffic jam.
